The test image shows a soybean stem split lengthwise with:
- White/cream colored pith internally
- Numerous small black specks on the stem exterior
- Grayish coloration of the internal tissue

Key candidates: Sudden_death_syndrome (white pith when split), Charcoal_Rot (black microsclerotia, charcoal-sprinkled appearance), Diaporthe (black pycnidia on stems). Let me check reference images.

The Charcoal_Rot reference top-left panel shows a nearly identical presentation — hand holding a split stem with grayish-white interior and black speckled exterior. Let me check a few more to confirm.
Now I have enough to make a confident comparison. Let me view a few more reference images to be thorough.

**Analysis summary:**

- **Test image**: Split soybean stem held in hand — white/gray pith internally, dense small black specks covering the stem exterior, grayish-brown outer tissue
- **Charcoal_Rot** reference (top-left panel): Nearly identical — hand holding split stem with grayish-white interior, exterior densely coated in tiny black specks (microsclerotia). The "charcoal-sprinkled" appearance matches perfectly
- **SDS**: Has white pith but exterior wouldn't show the dense black microsclerotia pattern; reference images focus on leaf interveinal chlorosis
- **Brown_Stem_Rot**: Pith should be brown (not white) when split
- **Diaporthe**: Shows pycnidia in linear rows on stem surface, different pattern
- **Fusarium/Phytophthora/Rhizoctonia**: All show different stem/root presentations with no charcoal-like speckling

The defining feature — dense, randomly scattered tiny black microsclerotia beneath and on the epidermis giving the charcoal-sprinkled appearance on a split stem — is the hallmark of Charcoal Rot.
